extracted.subtask_description: Practices and criteria for setting, communicating, and interpreting embargo times on press releases from scientific/medical journals. Focuses on time-zone handling, embargo duration, advance release for online-first articles, and press-office communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing the embargo to lift 30 minutes earlier in the US and Canada
rubrics_metrics.description: "We allow the embargo to lift 30 minutes earlier in real time in the US and Canada so that US east coast broadcasters can include news in their 1830H bulletins if they wish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit exception permitting a slightly earlier real-time embargo lift for North American broadcasters to accommodate evening newscasts; this is an intentional policy choice (in force since at least March 2007) and should be communicated clearly to recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily press release for online-first articles released at least 24 hours before online publication
rubrics_metrics.description: "A daily press release associated with the article in question will be released at least 24 hours before online publication." (The Lancet's embargo policy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal policy requires a 24-hour advance press release for online-first publications. Note: The Lancet's policy does not specify how journalists should use that time, whereas some journals (e.g., NEJM) explicitly state intended uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo duration should be long enough to be useful (preferably >48 hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique: "what’s the point of any embargo at all if it’s less than 48 hours?" — short embargoes (e.g., ~9 hours, NEJM's 4 hours) may not give journalists adequate time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer embargo periods give journalists time to prepare accurate coverage; very short embargoes often result from production delays and may undermine the value of embargoes. Consider setting embargoes that allow substantive reporting time (author preference expressed as 48+ hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one embargo time for all reporters (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion: "a journal has to choose one time for all reporters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in embargo timing avoids confusion among reporters in different regions or outlets. If exceptions exist, they should be explicitly documented and communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify the purpose and permitted uses of embargoed time
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: The Lancet "doesn’t specify what journalists use the time before embargo for, as NEJM does."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice is to state explicitly why embargoed access is being provided (e.g., to allow verification, expert interviews, preparation of coverage) so journalists understand and can use the time appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time zones and present embargo times unambiguously
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: "Keeping track of time zones when it comes to embargoes is tricky enough."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargo notices should specify time and timezone clearly (and, if applicable, how local real-time lifts are handled) to prevent misunderstandings across international newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid last-minute releases that shorten embargo windows where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation: Production/operational issues sometimes force a release on the same day, shortening the embargo (author and commentator note this caused short embargoes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational constraints should be minimized; if a late release is unavoidable, explain the reason and consider whether to maintain regular embargo timing or to notify recipients of any changes to preserve fairness and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt, candid press-office communication about embargo discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes appreciation for a "quick and candid response" from the Lancet press officer when asked about the discrepancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press officers should respond promptly and transparently to journalist queries about embargo times or exceptions to maintain trust and reduce confusion.
